title: Free or defended: who can really recapture?
outcomes: Counts only the pieces that can capture on a square as its defenders
Decides whether a capture is free, wins points or loses points
Does not treat a nearby enemy piece as a defender

steps.text: A piece is **defended** when a friendly piece could capture on its square and so take back. A piece nobody defends is **loose**, and taking it wins the piece unless the capture itself walks into something, so check that too. A black pawn captures down the board. The next board is the position you just tried: first the capture, then the answer.

steps.caption: The rook attacks the bishop on g5. The pawn on h6 defends it. The pawn on g6 stands in front of it but cannot capture on g5.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop for 3 points.
The h6 pawn recaptures. The g6 pawn could not have. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The bishop on e6 is loose: no black piece attacks that square. The knight can take it safely.

line.say: The knight takes the bishop and nothing can capture the knight there.
Nothing can retake here. White has won a bishop.

steps.text: A defender must be able to capture on that exact square, **using its own kind of move**. A pawn defends the two squares diagonally ahead of it. A knight defends by its jump, a bishop along its diagonals, a rook along its lines, and a queen both ways. A piece in the way blocks a line. Standing close counts for nothing. A **pinned** piece, one that cannot move without exposing its own king, does not count either.

steps.caption: A pawn defends diagonally forward. For Black, the pawn on d6 covers e5, so the knight is defended.

line.say: The rook takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The pawn takes back diagonally. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The black pawn on e4 is right below the knight, but pawns capture diagonally forward. It attacks d3 and f3, not e5.

line.say: The knight takes. The pawn on e4 cannot capture it, because pawns never capture straight ahead.
Nothing of Black's can take the knight. White has won a knight.

steps.caption: Black to move. A white pawn defends diagonally forward, which for White means up the board. The pawn on e4 covers d5.

line.say: The rook takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The white pawn takes back. Black gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The knight on f6 jumps to d5, so it defends the bishop.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop, winning 3 points.
The knight jumps to d5 and takes back. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The knight on e6 is one step from the bishop, but its jump does not reach d5. Close is not the same as defending.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop. The knight on e6 cannot reach d5.
Black has no recapture. White has won a bishop.

steps.caption: A bishop defends along its diagonals. The bishop on e6 and the knight on d5 touch corner to corner, so the knight is defended.

line.say: The queen takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The bishop takes back along the diagonal. White gave 9 for 3.

steps.caption: The d5 square is light. The black bishop on f8 stays on dark squares, so it can never capture there.

line.say: The queen takes the knight. The bishop on f8 cannot reach a light square.
Black has no way to take back. White has won a knight.

steps.caption: The rook on d8 faces the knight down the file, but its own pawn on d6 stands between them. A blocked line defends nothing.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. Black's rook cannot see past its own pawn.
Black cannot recapture. White has won a knight.

steps.caption: A clear long line does defend. The queen on b8 reaches e5 along the open diagonal, so the knight is defended from far away.

line.say: The rook takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The queen takes back along the diagonal. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The bishop on e6 touches the knight on d5, but the rook on e1 pins it to the king on e8. A pinned piece cannot capture, so it defends nothing.

line.say: The queen takes the knight. The bishop cannot retake, because moving it would expose its king.
Black cannot recapture. White has won a knight.

steps.text: Now suppose the target **is** defended. The capture may still be good, so compare what you win with what you lose when the defender takes back. Use the counting values: pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. **Rule of thumb:** a cheaper piece taking a dearer one usually gains, and a dearer piece taking a cheaper one loses. The values are only a guide.

**Net result = what you take, minus what you lose.** The capturing piece stands on the square, so it is the only thing a recapture can reach. A rook (5) takes a defended bishop (3): 3 - 5 = -2. A pawn (1) takes that bishop: 3 - 1 = +2. A knight (3) takes a defended knight: 3 - 3 = 0. **[I]** Beginners lose rooks to pawns because a rook feels powerful and the small pawn is easy to overlook.

steps.caption: The bishop is defended by a pawn, but a pawn is the cheapest piece. Taking a bishop with a pawn gains points even though it is retaken.

line.say: The pawn takes the bishop, winning 3 points.
The pawn retakes. White gave 1 and won 3, a gain of 2.

steps.caption: Now the other way round: a knight takes a defended pawn. The pawn on d6 will take back.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn, winning 1 point.
The pawn retakes the knight. White gave 3 for 1, a loss of 2.

steps.caption: Equal pieces on a defended square: knight for knight. Nobody gains points; whether to trade is a different question.

line.say: The knight takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The pawn retakes. White gave 3 and won 3, an even trade.

steps.title: Same capture, the defender changes
steps.prompt: Predict first: is the capture good when no piece defends the pawn, when a bishop defends it, and when a bishop stands nearby but cannot capture on that square?

steps.text: A **king** defends the eight squares around it, so it can take back too, as long as no other enemy piece covers the square it lands on. **[H]** My guess is that beginners count a nearby piece as a defender. Watch your own answers on the next items and see.

steps.caption: The king on d5 touches e4 and nothing of White's covers e4. The pawn is defended by the king.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn and lands next to the king.
The king takes the rook, since nothing covers e4. White gave 5 for 1.

steps.text: Count with care: point at each enemy piece that can really capture on the square, then at each of yours. Edward Lasker (Chess Strategy, our sheet K2, K3) told beginners to count attackers against defenders, and listed ways a defender can be an illusion: it can be pinned, captured by a cheaper piece, or called away. Today's blockers and wrong-colour bishops are simpler cases. Today there is one attacker.

steps.prompt: In two sentences, explain to a friend why a bishop standing next to a knight does not always defend it. Name one square where you once counted a defender that was not one.

steps.text: **Compare with your own words.** A piece is defended only if a friendly piece can really capture on its square: its own kind of move, with a clear line. A piece standing nearby, a bishop on the wrong square colour or a rook behind its own pawn does not count. If the target is defended, compare what you win with what you could lose.
